sources.title: Imam Ahmed Raza Khan and the Revival of the Islamic Astronomy in India
sources.author: Naseeb Ahmed Siddiqui
sources.publication: IIUM Journal of Religion and Civilisational Studies 6(1), 2023, pp. 57–83
sources.notes: Read in full (open-access PDF). Single-author article; the author was a PhD student when it was written (footnote, p. 57). The article says its own analysis of the astronomical works is introductory (p. 61), is sympathetic to its subject, and takes work counts from community websites (p. 62). Quotes the 1920 preface of Fauz-i-Mubin via a 2005 edition. Treat as one academic source, not as independent confirmation.

contributions.title: Critique of the 1919 planetary-alignment prediction (Mu'in-i-Mubin)
contributions.text: A treatise answering a published prediction of a planetary alignment, recalculating planetary positions on a geocentric model and arguing from gravitation against the predicted effects (as described in S1).
contributions.prior: A prediction by Albert F. Porta, based on heliocentric astronomy (per S1).
contributions.detail: A written response with its own geocentric calculation. Whether the calculation is sound has not been examined.
contributions.label: under_review

contributions.title: Arguments against the Earth's motion (Fauz-i-Mubin)
contributions.text: A book presenting 105 arguments, according to the author's preface as quoted in S1, against the motion of the Earth, drawing on mathematics, philosophy, logic and the physics of his day. It is a historical argument. Modern astronomy establishes that the Earth rotates and orbits the Sun, so its conclusion is not part of modern astronomy.
contributions.prior: Copernican and Newtonian astronomy; earlier Muslim astronomical critique of Greek models (per S1).
contributions.detail: A systematic polemical argument against Earth's motion and against attraction/repulsion explanations. Originality of individual arguments is the author's own claim and unverified.
contributions.label: under_review

claims.text: Born in 1856 in Bareilly.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Year and place only. Day-level date (14 June 1856) appears only on Wikipedia-derived pages: UNVERIFIED.
claims.needs: Confirm in Sanyal or a primary biography.

claims.text: Death in 1921 (day-level date reported as 28 October 1921 / 25 Safar 1340 AH on Wikipedia-derived pages).
claims.label: UNVERIFIED
claims.note: S1 does not state the death date. The 1856–1921 range comes from the project brief. Different Wikipedia versions disagree ("October 1921" vs "28 October 1921"), which supports leaving the day-level date unverified.
claims.needs: Confirm in Sanyal or a reference work.

claims.text: His father, Maulana Naqi Ali Khan, gave his early education; his grandfather Riza Ali turned from a soldier's path to religious study.
claims.label: UNDER REVIEW
claims.note: Stated in S1 without a direct citation in that passage.
claims.needs: Check against Sanyal and the biography by Zafar ud-Din Bihari (1938).

claims.text: Traditional account that he became a scholar at age 13 years 10 months.
claims.label: UNVERIFIED
claims.note: Traditional narrative repeated in S1.
claims.needs: Find an independent or primary record.

claims.text: Scholars of Makkah and Madinah are said to have titled him Mujaddid (reviver) of the 14th Hijri century.
claims.label: UNVERIFIED
claims.note: S1 attributes this to Hallaq 1984, Sahab 1997 and Zafar ud-Din 1938. Whether those works support it has not been checked (Hallaq's article, as cited in S1, is on ijtihad).

claims.text: He is said to have written over 1,000 books on 50+ branches of knowledge; S1 lists approximate counts per field taken from alahazrat.net.
claims.label: UNVERIFIED
claims.note: ISA does not state a total number of works.
claims.needs: Needs a bibliography built from catalogues.

claims.text: His student Zafaruddin Bihari is reported to have told him of the 1919 prediction (S1 p. 63); Bihari also wrote the 1938 biography Hayat-e A'la Hazrat (S1 p. 83).
claims.label: UNDER REVIEW
claims.note: Teacher–student relationship is a lead; relationships will be recorded only with support.

claims.text: S1 reports that an institute devoted to him states 21 PhD and six master's dissertations exist on his works.
claims.label: UNVERIFIED
claims.note: Institutional self-report; not checked.

claims.text: In October 1919 an American, Albert F. Porta, predicted a planetary alignment for 17 December 1919 with claimed effects on the Sun and Earth; S1 cites 1919 newspapers.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Newspaper citations in S1 have not been checked.

claims.text: S1 lists four treatises prompted by the prediction: Mu'in-i-Mubin (1919), Fauz-i-Mubin Dar Radd-i-Harkat-i-Zamin (1920), Al-Kalimah al-Mulhamah (1920), Nuzul-i-Ayat-i-Furqan (1921).
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Years conflict with another listing that dates the earth-motion treatises to 1919 (retail/devotional page). Original-script titles not verified.

claims.text: Mu'in-i-Mubin was written to refute Porta's predictions; it was first published in a magazine and later compiled into a short treatise.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: In it he calculated planetary positions for 17 December 1919 on a geocentric model and reported a mutual separation of about 122°, against Porta's 26°.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Description of what S1 reports. The calculation itself has not been examined.

claims.text: He argued that if gravitation holds, the combined pull of six planets could not destroy the Sun while sparing larger planets; he also cited earlier sunspot observations, including by Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi.
claims.label: UNDER REVIEW
claims.note: The attributions to earlier astronomers are as reported in S1 and are unchecked.

claims.text: Per S1's quotation of the author's preface, Fauz-i-Mubin has a foreword, four chapters and a conclusion, and presents 105 arguments against Earth's motion (12 on repulsion, 50 on attraction, 43 in a third chapter); he says 15 were discussed in earlier books.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: Structure and count are the author's own statement as quoted in S1 (2005 edition, pp. 8–9). Not checked against a primary edition. His claim that 90 are original is self-assessment: UNVERIFIED.

claims.text: S1 describes Fauz-i-Mubin as a mathematical, astronomical, philosophical and logical refutation of Copernican astronomy; it criticises the law of universal gravitation and discusses weight, attraction, repulsion and tides.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED
claims.note: S1's characterisation, not ISA's evaluation.

claims.text: He also disputed ancient and medieval arguments for a static Earth and treated that material in Al-Kalimah al-Mulhamah.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: Nuzul-i-Ayat-i-Furqan arose from a fatwa request dated 23 January 1921 and argues from Qur'anic verses and hadith that the Earth and heavens are stationary.
claims.label: ACADEMICALLY SUPPORTED

claims.text: S1 judges that he was not the first critic of Copernicus but was distinctive in arguing from gravitation and tide theory; S1 also calls him a mathematician and astronomer.
claims.label: UNDER REVIEW
claims.note: These are the article author's judgements. Independent documentation of mathematical or astronomical work beyond these treatises has not yet been found.
claims.needs: Independent scholarship on his mathematics and astronomy.

claims.text: S1 cites a 2006 English-titled work, 'Warding off the foulness in understanding the time', and quotes a remark about a >15° difference from true dawn.
claims.label: UNVERIFIED
claims.note: Original title and subject unknown; possibly timekeeping or prayer-time related.

claims.text: Modern astronomy establishes that the Earth rotates on its axis and orbits the Sun.
claims.label: MODERN SCIENTIFIC ASSESSMENT
claims.note: Drafted by ISA from standard knowledge; no citation attached yet.
claims.needs: Cite an astronomy textbook or reference.

claims.text: That no catastrophe followed 17 December 1919 does not discriminate between geocentric and heliocentric descriptions of the planets' motion.
claims.label: MODERN SCIENTIFIC ASSESSMENT
claims.note: Drafted by ISA. S1 (p. 66) states no catastrophe occurred and reads this as supporting the geocentric model; ISA records that reading as S1's.

claims.text: OPEN QUESTION: the 26° and 122° figures may measure different things (angular positions depend on the observer's location, e.g. seen from the Sun versus from Earth). Whether they are comparable must be checked against the primary text and historical ephemerides.
claims.label: MODERN SCIENTIFIC ASSESSMENT
claims.note: No conclusion drawn.

claims.text: Earth's distance from the Sun does vary by roughly 5 million km (about 3.1 million miles) over the year, comparable to the figure S1 quotes from the work; in modern physics this is explained by a bound elliptical orbit under inverse-square gravity, not by a contradiction in attraction.
claims.label: MODERN SCIENTIFIC ASSESSMENT
claims.note: Drafted by ISA; figures need a citation.
claims.needs: Cite Kepler's laws and orbital data from a textbook.

claims.text: Modern theory attributes tides to the difference in the Moon's gravity across the Earth (the tide-raising force, falling off with the cube of distance), not to the Moon's total pull compared with Earth's own gravity on the water.
claims.label: MODERN SCIENTIFIC ASSESSMENT
claims.note: Drafted by ISA. S1 (p. 73) calls the work's tide argument valid; ISA records that as the article author's opinion only.
claims.needs: Cite an oceanography or astronomy reference.

Find independent scholarship on his mathematics (logarithms, algebra, geometry works are listed only by count on community sites) and on his timekeeping or prayer-time work.
Check the 1919 newspaper reports cited in S1 and the historical ephemerides for 17 Dec 1919.
Obtain astronomy and physics textbook citations for M-001 to M-005 from a qualified reviewer.
Human translation review for Urdu/Arabic versions.
